entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The People's Crusade was a pivotal event in the complex tapestry of medieval history, marking a catastrophic attempt by a poor people's army to reclaim Jerusalem from Muslim Turks in 1095-1100. Led by Peter the Hermit and Walter Sans-Avoir, the crusade unfolded in Central Europe, entangling the faith, politics, and lives of countless individuals.

The crusade was sparked by a call to arms from Pope Urban II, who rallied a disaffected population to march on the holy city. With a fervor that bordered on the fanatical, the People's Crusade converged on Jerusalem in the spring of 1096, only to suffer a crushing defeat at the hands of the Seljuk Turks. The once-mighty crusader army lay decimated, leaving behind a tragic legacy of death, displacement, and disillusionment.

The aftermath of the People's Crusade saw a re-evaluation of the crusading movement, with many questioning the efficacy of such violent endeavors. As the century progressed, the memory of the crusade would serve as a cautionary tale, underscoring the perils of unchecked fervor and the devastating consequences of unbridled violence. The People's Crusade serves as a poignant reminder of the complexities and uncertainties of medieval society.

As the 12th century drew to a close, the memory of the People's Crusade lingered as a haunting reminder of the darker aspects of human nature. In the words of historian Albert of Aachen, 'the People's Crusade was a great calamity, a disaster that shook the very foundations of Christendom.'
